THE TEACHER WHO DRIVES TWO HOURS TO SCHOOL

Every Monday morning, Lin Yu-ting leaves her home in the city before dawn and drives nearly two hours into the mountains of Nantou County. She is not commuting to her own job in the usual sense; she is the only science teacher for three small elementary schools scattered across a remote township.

Ten years ago, Lin was working at a large school in Taichung with more than forty students in each class. She decided to apply for a special rural teaching program after reading that some mountain schools had fewer than ten students total and no teacher qualified to teach science at all.

Her weekly routine now looks unusual. She spends Monday and Tuesday at one school, Wednesday and Thursday at another, and Friday at the third, carrying a box of simple lab equipment in her car trunk. Students who once only read about experiments in textbooks now get to mix chemicals and grow plants themselves.

Lin says the hardest part is not the driving but the goodbyes; students often move away when their parents find work elsewhere. Still, she has no plans to return to the city. "These students deserve the same chances as anyone else," she says, "even if it takes an extra two hours each way to give it to them."

THE HIDDEN COST OF A FIVE-DOLLAR T-SHIRT

Walk into almost any fast fashion store and you will find T-shirts priced lower than a cup of coffee. For many shoppers, especially teenagers on a tight budget, these prices feel like a bargain. But cheap clothing often carries a cost that does not appear on the price tag.

Fast fashion brands release new clothing collections every few weeks instead of every season, encouraging customers to buy constantly and throw away clothes quickly. Producing this much clothing requires huge amounts of water, energy, and chemical dye, much of which ends up polluting rivers near factories.

Workers pay a price too. Investigations have repeatedly found that some factories supplying fast fashion brands pay workers extremely low wages for long hours in unsafe conditions. Brands often respond by promising reform, but critics say real change happens slowly, if at all.

Some young consumers have started pushing back, choosing secondhand clothing or repairing old items instead of buying new ones every month. Online secondhand marketplaces have grown quickly in Taiwan over the past few years, suggesting that at least some shoppers are rethinking their habits.

Still, changing an entire industry built on speed and low prices will take far more than a shift among a few environmentally conscious teenagers.

explain_zh: 文章說明快時尚看似便宜，卻在環境與勞工方面付出代價，即使有年輕人開始改變習慣，整體產業要改變仍需要更多努力，C 最能概括全文。A、B、D 都與文章內容不符。主旨題要注意文章標題「hidden cost」點出的重點。

WHY MORE PEOPLE ARE POURING PLANT MILK INTO THEIR COFFEE

Walk into any coffee shop in Taiwan today, and you will likely see oat milk, soy milk, and almond milk listed as alternatives to regular dairy milk. A decade ago, plant-based milk was mostly limited to soy milk sold at breakfast shops. Now it fills entire refrigerator sections in supermarkets.

Several factors explain this shift. Some drinkers switch to plant milk because they are lactose intolerant, meaning their bodies struggle to digest the sugar found naturally in cow's milk. Others choose plant milk for environmental reasons, since producing dairy milk generally requires far more land and water than growing oats or soybeans.

Not all plant milks are equal, however. Oat milk tends to be higher in carbohydrates than dairy milk, while almond milk is naturally low in protein unless companies add extra nutrients during production. Nutritionists recommend checking the label rather than assuming that any plant milk is automatically healthier than dairy.

Coffee shops have noticed the trend too. Baristas say oat milk has become especially popular because it foams similarly to dairy milk, making it useful for lattes and cappuccinos. Some cafés even charge extra for plant milk, a policy that has sparked debate among regular customers who feel they are being charged more for choosing a different option.

options: Because dairy milk has recently become more expensive than plant milk everywhere

Because they are lactose intolerant or concerned about environmental impact
Because government regulations now require all cafés to offer plant milk
explain_zh: 文中提到部分人因為乳糖不耐或環境考量而改喝植物奶，故選C。A、B、D 文章都沒有提到，屬於捏造的細節。細節題只要找到列出原因的那段文字即可作答。

WHO OWNS A PICTURE THAT AN AI DID NOT ENTIRELY CREATE?

Type a few words into an AI art generator, and within seconds you can receive a detailed digital painting that once would have taken a human artist days to finish. These tools have become popular among students, hobbyists, and even professional designers looking for quick inspiration. They have also sparked one of the most heated debates in the creative world today.

Supporters argue that AI art tools simply extend what technology has always done: making creative work more accessible. A student without expensive art training can now produce illustrations for a school project or a small business logo. Supporters also note that a human still chooses the words that guide the AI, so some creativity remains involved.

Critics see the issue differently. Many AI art generators were trained using millions of images scraped from the internet, often without asking the original artists for permission. Some illustrators say their personal art style has been copied by AI tools trained on their work, without payment or credit given to them.

Courts in several countries are now trying to decide whether AI-generated images can be copyrighted at all, and whether using copyrighted art to train AI counts as theft or simply learning, the way a human artist studies other painters. No clear answer has emerged yet, leaving artists and companies in a legal grey area.

options: AI art generators have been completely banned in most countries around the world

Courts have already decided that AI-generated images can never be copyrighted
explain_zh: 文章介紹AI繪圖工具帶來的便利，也提到創作者權益、著作權等爭議尚無定論，B 最能涵蓋全文重點。A、D 與文章內容不符（法院尚未有定論）；C 文章沒有這樣的主張。主旨題要注意文章結尾強調「沒有明確答案」。

For many travellers, no trip to Taiwan feels complete without a visit to a night market. These lively streets, usually busiest after sunset, pack together food stalls, games, and small shops selling everything from clothing to phone cases.

Whether you are chasing a specific dish or simply want to soak in the atmosphere, a night market offers one of the most authentic tastes of everyday life in Taiwan.

More than eight hundred volunteers gathered along Taiwan's northeast coast last weekend for one of the largest beach cleanups held in the region this year. By the end of the day, organisers reported collecting more than two tonnes of trash, ranging from plastic bottles to broken fishing nets.

The event, organised jointly by an environmental group and several local schools, aimed to raise awareness about ocean pollution while directly removing waste from the coastline. Volunteers worked in small teams, each assigned a specific section of beach, and sorted collected items into categories such as plastic, glass, and metal for recycling.

Environmental scientists say much of the trash found on Taiwan's beaches does not originate locally. Ocean currents carry plastic waste from other countries across the Pacific, meaning that even a perfectly clean local beach could still be covered in debris within weeks. This makes ongoing cleanups necessary rather than a one-time solution.

Fishing gear made up a surprisingly large portion of the collected waste. Abandoned or lost nets, sometimes called "ghost nets," can continue trapping fish and other marine animals for years after being discarded. Several volunteers said finding these nets tangled with dead sea creatures was the most upsetting part of the day.

Organisers plan to hold similar cleanups quarterly, hoping that regular events will keep pace with the constant arrival of new waste.

More than eight hundred volunteers gathered along Taiwan's northeast coast last weekend for one of the largest beach cleanups held in the region this year. By the end of the day, organisers reported collecting more than two tonnes of trash, ranging from plastic bottles to broken fishing nets.

The event, organised jointly by an environmental group and several local schools, aimed to raise awareness about ocean pollution while directly removing waste from the coastline. Volunteers worked in small teams, each assigned a specific section of beach, and sorted collected items into categories such as plastic, glass, and metal for recycling.

Environmental scientists say much of the trash found on Taiwan's beaches does not originate locally. Ocean currents carry plastic waste from other countries across the Pacific, meaning that even a perfectly clean local beach could still be covered in debris within weeks. This makes ongoing cleanups necessary rather than a one-time solution.

Fishing gear made up a surprisingly large portion of the collected waste. Abandoned or lost nets, sometimes called "ghost nets," can continue trapping fish and other marine animals for years after being discarded. Several volunteers said finding these nets tangled with dead sea creatures was the most upsetting part of the day.

Organisers plan to hold similar cleanups quarterly, hoping that regular events will keep pace with the constant arrival of new waste.

GREEN ROOFS: A QUIET SOLUTION FOR HOT CITIES

As Taiwanese cities grow warmer each summer, architects and urban planners are increasingly turning to an old idea with new relevance: green roofs. Rather than covering a building's top with plain concrete or asphalt, a green roof is layered with soil and planted with vegetation, ranging from simple grasses to small shrubs.

The benefits extend beyond appearance. A layer of soil and plants insulates a building far more effectively than bare concrete, reducing indoor temperatures during summer and cutting air-conditioning costs. On a larger scale, green roofs across a city can help offset the urban heat island effect, in which cities trap heat and become noticeably hotter than surrounding rural areas.

Green roofs also absorb rainwater during storms, slowing the rate at which water reaches drainage systems and reducing the risk of flash flooding in low-lying neighbourhoods. Some studies suggest that a well-designed green roof can absorb up to seventy percent of the rain that falls on it.

Despite these advantages, adoption remains slow. Installing a green roof costs significantly more than a conventional one, and older buildings often lack the structural strength to support the extra weight of soil and water. Government subsidies in a few cities have begun encouraging adoption, but experts argue that without stronger building codes requiring green roofs on new construction, progress will likely remain gradual rather than widespread.

CAN A ROBOT KEEP AN ELDERLY PERSON COMPANY?

In a small apartment in New Taipei City, an eighty-three-year-old woman named Mrs. Lai chats every afternoon with a round, white robot about the size of a basketball. The robot, developed by a Taiwanese technology company, reminds her to take her medication, asks how she slept, and can call her daughter automatically if it detects that she has fallen.

Companion robots like this one are becoming more common as Taiwan's population ages and fewer families have someone available to check on elderly relatives during the day. Sensors built into the robot track movement patterns around the apartment; unusual patterns, such as no movement detected for several hours, trigger an alert sent to family members or a care centre.

Researchers studying these robots note a surprising benefit beyond safety monitoring. Many elderly users report feeling less lonely, since the robot asks simple conversational questions and responds to short answers. For someone who lives alone, even a limited daily exchange can reduce feelings of isolation.

Critics caution that companion robots should supplement, not replace, real human contact. A robot cannot provide the emotional depth of a conversation with a family member or friend, and some worry that families might rely on robots to avoid visiting elderly relatives in person. Developers respond that the technology is meant to fill gaps, not to substitute entirely for human relationships.

Play a recorded message reminding her to stand up carefully
explain_zh: 文中提到機器人「can call her daughter automatically if it detects that she has fallen」，故選B。A、C、D 文章都沒有提到這些功能。細節題直接對照原文列出的功能敘述即可判斷。
